MSK–SKIN · WEEK 15 · LECTURE COMPANION

Bone Growth, Formation, & Fractures

Meghan McGee-Lawrence, Ph.D. · October 26, 2026 · Course-first teaching with selective Step 1 connections

Learning objectives

  1. Compare intramembranous and endochondral ossification.
  2. Recognize growth plate morphology and zones.
  3. Explain fracture repair sequence and timing.
  4. Identify synovial joint tissues and joint cavity components.
  5. Explain osteoarthritis pathophysiology.

Big picture · how the processes connect

Bone can be made directly from mesenchyme (intramembranous) or by replacing a temporary cartilage template (endochondral). The growth plate uses the latter mechanism to lengthen long bones; fracture repair often reenacts it. Synovial joints preserve articular cartilage at bone ends, where wear and failed tissue maintenance drive osteoarthritis.

Must knowBone length depends on cartilage proliferation and replacement at the physis. Bone diameter increases by appositional deposition on periosteal/endosteal surfaces. Both pathways initially form woven bone, subsequently remodeled to lamellar bone.

Objective 1 · two routes to make bone

Intramembranous ossification · no cartilage intermediate

Mesenchymal cells condense and differentiate directly into osteoblast progenitors. Osteoblasts release unmineralized osteoid; calcium–phosphate deposition mineralizes this matrix. Woven spicules merge into trabeculae (spongy bone), while deposition beneath the periosteum creates compact cortical tables. Remodeling replaces woven with lamellar bone.

Mesenchymal condensation → osteoblast → osteoid → mineralization → woven trabeculae → lamellar remodeling
Clinical connectionDistraction osteogenesis and strongly stabilized fracture repair can use direct intramembranous bone formation with little or no cartilaginous callus. Mechanical stability therefore influences which repair pathway predominates.

Endochondral ossification · cartilage first, bone second

Mesenchyme forms a hyaline cartilage model. A diaphyseal bone collar develops. Deep chondrocytes hypertrophy, cartilage matrix calcifies, chondrocytes die, and vessels invade with osteoprogenitor cells. Osteoblasts deposit osteoid onto remaining calcified-cartilage scaffolds, creating the primary diaphyseal ossification center. The marrow cavity expands as central tissue is remodeled; secondary centers appear in epiphyses. Cartilage persists at articular surfaces and between epiphysis and metaphysis as the physis.

IntramembranousEndochondral
PrecursorMesenchyme directly → boneHyaline cartilage model → bone
Typical sitesFlat cranial bones; parts of clavicleLong bones; short and irregular bones
Critical cellsOsteoblast differentiationChondrocyte growth → hypertrophy → calcification + vascular invasion
Clinical linkRigidly stabilized healing; distraction osteogenesisPhyses, secondary fracture repair, heterotopic ossification
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · What is the single defining difference between these pathways?

Intramembranous bone is deposited directly in mesenchyme; endochondral bone replaces a cartilage template.

Objective 2 · the growth plate as a conveyor belt

The epiphyseal plate (physis) is a cartilaginous zone between the epiphysis and metaphysis. Its organization is spatially readable from epiphysis toward diaphysis. Each step generates the next region of longitudinal growth.

From epiphysis → metaphysisWhat happensWhat it looks like
Resting / reserveRelatively quiescent chondrocytes support the growth plate.Small cells scattered in hyaline matrix.
ProliferativeChondrocytes divide → new rows elongate cartilage template.Flattened, orderly stacks/columns.
HypertrophicChondrocytes enlarge; matrix becomes thin between cells.Large lacunae, tall columns.
Cell death + calcificationMatrix calcifies, cells die, capillaries invade.Residual calcified-cartilage scaffold.
Bone deposition → resorptionOsteoblasts lay bone on cartilage cores; osteoclasts remodel trabeculae.Developing metaphyseal bone trabeculae.
Common confusionLength vs width: the physis lengthens long bones through cartilage-to-bone replacement; periosteal and endosteal apposition adjusts diameter. After physeal closure, longitudinal growth stops.

Clinical consequences of altered endochondral signaling

Achondroplasia: constitutively active FGFR3 limits chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation, creating narrow/disorganized proliferative and hypertrophic growth plate zones; limbs are shortened relative to the trunk. This is a growth-plate defect, not failure of osteoblast mineralization.

Myositis ossificans (MO): benign, often self-limited heterotopic ossification after blunt or repetitive muscle trauma. Injury → cytokines (TGF/BMP) → endothelial–mesenchymal transition → osteochondral differentiation → cartilage-mediated bone deposition in muscle. Expect pain, stiffness, limited adjacent-joint range of motion.

Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP): genetic ACVR1 mutation (encoding ALK2 BMP type I receptor) increases BMP pathway signaling and drives progressive ectopic endochondral bone formation in soft connective tissues. The bone is qualitatively normal but abnormally located.

Exam trapMO versus FOP: isolated, injury-associated, often resolving MO versus inherited, progressive ACVR1-associated FOP. Both may build heterotopic bone through an endochondral pathway.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Which growth plate zone drives longitudinal expansion, and what happens in achondroplasia?

Chondrocytes proliferate in ordered columns; activating FGFR3 narrows/disorganizes proliferative and hypertrophic zones, reducing long-bone growth.

Objective 3 · fracture healing and how to describe fractures

Fracture breaks bone and surrounding vessels; repair first creates a stable biological bridge, then replaces it with mechanically efficient mature tissue. The phases overlap rather than occur in isolated blocks.

PhaseApproximate timing shown in lectureKey events
Hematoma / inflammationHours → daysBleeding, clot, cellular injury and inflammatory signaling.
Granulation / fibrovascular repair~2–12 days (depicted)Capillary ingrowth, fibroblasts and mesenchymal precursors; inflammatory bridge becomes vascularized tissue.
Soft callus~1 week → several monthsFibrocartilage and cartilage stabilize fracture ends.
Hard callus~several weeks → monthsChondrocytes hypertrophy, cartilage calcifies, vessels invade, woven trabecular bone replaces soft callus.
RemodelingMonths → yearsWoven bone becomes lamellar; extra callus resorbed; medullary/cortical shape and load response recover.
Must knowThe phrase soft callus → hard callus is endochondral ossification in miniature: cartilage must be calcified and invaded by blood vessels before bone replaces it. Very rigidly stabilized fracture fragments may instead heal by direct intramembranous pathways.

Clinical signs and language

Typical fracture findings: pain, swelling/tenderness, bruising, deformity, and sometimes visible skin disruption. A bone can be broken without a dramatic visible deformity. Describe a fracture across several independent axes:

DimensionDistinctions that matter
Line orientationTransverse (across), oblique (diagonal), longitudinal (along), spiral (torsional).
Special morphologyGreenstick (one cortex breaks, other bends); torus/buckle (cortex buckles); compression (crushed/collapsed bone).
Fragment positionDisplacement (offset), angulation (deviation), shortening (overlap), rotation (twist). Can coexist.
CountSimple = two fragments; comminuted = >2.
Skin communicationClosed = no communication; open/compound = communicates with atmosphere, even if bone is not visible.

Stabilization and repair

Reduction restores fragment alignment. Immobilization helps maintain healing position. The lecture illustrates cast immobilization, functional brace/splint (controlled movement), traction, external fixation (pins connected externally), and open reduction/internal fixation (plates, screws, intramedullary rods).

Vertebral compression fractures

Frequently fragility-related in older patients. Clinical clues include focal axial pain, localized spinous tenderness, and new kyphosis from vertebral collapse; radiographs may demonstrate loss of vertebral height. The lecture defines radiographic loss of height as ≥20% or at least 4 mm and describes conservative management/bracing and selective procedural options.

ProcedureKey distinction
VertebroplastyInject cement directly into compressed bone; lecture describes relatively higher injection pressure.
KyphoplastyBalloon expands cavity / may recover height; fill cavity with cement at relatively lower pressure.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Which fracture morphology suggests torsion? How can a fracture be open without a visibly protruding bone?

Spiral fracture suggests torsional loading. Open fracture means the fracture communicates with outside air through breached skin; no protrusion is required.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · What tissue replaces soft callus?

Hard callus of immature/woven bone formed through endochondral replacement of cartilage; later remodeled to stronger lamellar architecture.

Objective 4 · what is actually in a synovial joint?

Diarthrodial (synovial) joints prioritize mobility with low surface friction. The ends of bones are covered by hyaline articular cartilage, which lacks blood vessels and perichondrium; this limits its capacity to regenerate following injury. A strong fibrous outer capsule encloses the joint, with localized thickening contributing ligaments. Its inner synovial membrane borders the cavity and contributes to synovial fluid, which contains hyaluronic acid and lubricin for low-friction movement.

Common confusionThe synovial membrane does not cover the articular cartilage surface. The articular cartilage faces synovial fluid in the cavity, while synovium lines the noncartilaginous inner capsule.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Which two synovial-fluid constituents reduce friction, and why does cartilage heal poorly?

Hyaluronic acid and lubricin aid lubrication. Articular hyaline cartilage is avascular and lacks a perichondrium.

Objective 5 · osteoarthritis (OA) is a whole-joint degeneration

OA begins as mechanically and biologically mediated failure of articular cartilage maintenance, rather than primarily inflammatory synovitis. The lecture emphasizes depletion/disruption of proteoglycans, water content, and type II collagen fibrils, permitting surface fissures and progressive cartilage loss. Loading then transmits through altered joint surfaces; subchondral sclerosis, osteophytes, joint-capsule and synovial changes, and cyst formation follow.

Cartilage matrix deterioration → surface tears + thinning → reduced joint space → altered loading → subchondral thickening / osteophytes → pain, reduced function, deformity

Risk factors taught: older age, previous joint injury/overuse, female sex, obesity and genetic factors. Frequently affected joints: hands, hips and knees. The lecture discusses severe disease treated with total joint arthroplasty when conservative strategies no longer provide satisfactory results.

Lecture → Step 1 bridgeLoss of radiographic joint space is an indirect indicator of cartilage loss because hyaline cartilage itself is not radiopaque. Osteophytes + subchondral sclerosis support a degenerative process. This uses the professor’s imaging pattern without importing unrelated rheumatology.
First Aid connectionOA tends to produce mechanical joint symptoms (pain with activity, limited range of motion, brief stiffness after rest). This board presentation complements, rather than substitutes for, the lecture’s cartilage/whole-joint pathogenesis.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · What three findings should you seek on an OA radiograph?

Joint-space narrowing, subchondral thickening/sclerosis, and osteophytes; advanced cases can show deformation.

Master these before moving on

  1. Direct bone vs cartilage template: never confuse intramembranous and endochondral formation.
  2. Growth plate sequence: resting → proliferation → hypertrophy → calcification/death → vascular invasion → bone formation/remodeling.
  3. Callus sequence: hematoma → granulation → soft cartilaginous bridge → woven bone → lamellar remodeling.
  4. Joint tissue boundaries: hyaline cartilage, capsule, synovial lining, synovial cavity and fluid are distinct.
  5. OA tissue-to-image connection: cartilage breakdown produces narrowing; abnormal load produces sclerotic bone and osteophytes.

Most useful First Aid connections

  • FGFR3 activation → restricted chondrocyte growth → achondroplasia and rhizomelic limb shortening.
  • ACVR1/ALK2 signaling → progressive heterotopic ossification (FOP), versus trauma-linked localized MO.
  • Secondary fracture healing recapitulates endochondral ossification.
  • Osteoporotic fragility → vertebral compression fracture (link to prior non-neoplastic bone lecture).
  • OA → narrowed joint space, sclerosis and osteophytes.
